## Introduction

The vignette *Actuarial Present Value and IRR Analysis*
(`vignette("apv-analysis", package = "abslife")`) shows how to calculate the
actuarial present value (APV) and the risk-adjusted internal rate of return
(IRR) of one loan. It can also be useful to calculate them for every loan in a
portfolio. For example, the sum of the loan APVs estimates the price of the
portfolio, which investors can compare with its market price. The IRRs of the
loans also show how the risk-adjusted return changes from one risk category to
another [@lautier2024convergence].

The `aloans` data set has `r format(nrow(aloans), big.mark = ",")` loans, so
calculating them one after another can take several minutes. The calculation for
one loan does not depend on the other loans. Thus, the computer can calculate
several loans at the same time. This vignette shows how to do that to save time.


## Data preparation

We label the event types and treat the loans that are censored at the largest
observed lifetime as prepaid. We also list the risk categories, from the
riskiest to the least risky.

```{r data}
library(abslife)
library(parallel) ## for parallel computations
library(ggplot2)  ## for plots

data(aloans)
data(aloans_recov)

aloans <- transform(aloans,
                    event_type = ifelse(D == 1, "Default", "Prepayment"))
at_end <- which(aloans$Z == max(aloans$Z) & aloans$C == 1)
aloans$C[at_end] <- 0
aloans$R[at_end] <- 1

categories <- c("deep_subprime", "subprime", "near_prime",
                "prime", "super_prime")
```

The function `detectCores()` returns the number of processor cores, that is, the
number of calculations that the computer can do at the same time. We use all
cores but one, so that the computer stays responsive.

```{r cores}
num_cores <- max(1L, detectCores() - 1L, na.rm = TRUE)
```

## The calculation for one loan

The function `loan_metrics()` calculates the APV and the IRR of loan `i` in the
data frame `loans`. Its arguments `hazard` and `recov` are the hazard estimates
and the recovery curve of the risk category of the loan. The largest observed
lifetime in `aloans` is `r max(aloans$Z)` months, but some loans have longer
terms. For these loans, `calculate_apv()` and `solve_irr()` extrapolate the
hazards and give a warning. The function hides these warnings, because they
repeat for many loans.

```{r loan-metrics}
loan_metrics <- function(i, loans, hazard, recov) {
  apv <- suppressWarnings(
    calculate_apv(x = hazard,
                  cur_age = loans$Z[i],
                  orig_term = loans$orig.term[i],
                  orig_loan_amt = loans$orig.loan.amt[i],
                  mon_pmt = loans$calc.pmt[i],
                  ref_rate = 0.05,
                  recov_curve = recov,
                  orig_apy = loans$orig.apr[i])
  )
  irr <- suppressWarnings(
    solve_irr(x = hazard,
              abs0_bal = loans$abs0.balance[i],
              cur_age = max(min(hazard$lifetime), loans$abs0.age[i]),
              orig_term = loans$orig.term[i],
              orig_loan_amt = loans$orig.loan.amt[i],
              mon_pmt = loans$calc.pmt[i],
              recov_curve = recov,
              orig_apy = loans$orig.apr[i])
  )
  c(apv = apv$APV, irr = irr$annualized_rate)
}
```

Each risk category has its own hazard estimates and recovery curve. We split the
loans and the recovery curves by risk category, and we estimate the hazards for
each category.

```{r hazards, warning = FALSE}
loans_by_cat <- split(aloans, aloans$risk.cat)[categories]
recov_by_cat <- split(aloans_recov, aloans_recov$risk.cat)[categories]
hazard_by_cat <- lapply(loans_by_cat, function(loans) {
  estimate_hazard(lifetime = loans$Z,
                  trunc_time = loans$Y,
                  censoring_indicator = loans$C,
                  event_type = loans$event_type,
                  ci_level = 0.95,
                  carry_hazard = FALSE)
})
```

## Running the calculations in parallel

The code depends on the operating system. Both versions give the same result: a
list, `results_list`, with one data frame for each risk category.

### macOS and Linux

The function `mclapply()` works like `lapply()`, but it runs the calculations
for several loans at the same time. Its argument `mc.cores` sets the number of
calculations that run at the same time.

```{r unix, eval = .Platform$OS.type == "unix"}
results_list <- lapply(categories, function(rc) {
  loans <- loans_by_cat[[rc]]
  metrics <- mclapply(seq_len(nrow(loans)), loan_metrics,
                      loans = loans,
                      hazard = hazard_by_cat[[rc]],
                      recov = recov_by_cat[[rc]],
                      mc.cores = num_cores)
  cbind(loans, do.call(rbind, metrics))
})
```

### Windows

On Windows, `mclapply()` can run only one calculation at a time. Instead,
`makeCluster()` starts several R sessions in the background, and `parLapply()`
divides the loans among them. Each session must load `abslife` before it can
calculate. At the end, `stopCluster()` closes the sessions.

```{r windows, eval = .Platform$OS.type == "windows"}
cl <- makeCluster(num_cores)
## loading abslife at each session
invisible(clusterEvalQ(cl, library(abslife)))
results_list <- lapply(categories, function(rc) {
  loans <- loans_by_cat[[rc]]
  metrics <- parLapply(cl, seq_len(nrow(loans)), loan_metrics,
                       loans = loans,
                       hazard = hazard_by_cat[[rc]],
                       recov = recov_by_cat[[rc]])
  cbind(loans, do.call(rbind, metrics))
})
stopCluster(cl)
```

## Results

We combine the results and give the risk categories readable labels.

```{r results}
results <- do.call(rbind, results_list)
results$risk.cat <- factor(results$risk.cat,
                           levels = categories,
                           labels = c("deep subprime", "subprime",
                                      "near-prime", "prime", "super-prime"))
```

The sum of the loan APVs, \$`r format(round(sum(results$apv)), big.mark = ",")`,
estimates the price of the portfolio. The plot below shows the APVs by risk
category.

```{r apv-plot, fig.cap = "APV of the loans by risk category."}
ggplot(results,
       aes(x = risk.cat,
           y = apv)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "gray70",
               outlier.alpha = .5) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Risk Category",
       y = "APV")
```

The next plot shows the annualized IRRs by risk category. To make the boxes
easier to read, it leaves out the `r sum(results$irr >= 0.4)` loans with an IRR
of 40% or more. For a financial analysis of these results, see
@lautier2024convergence.

```{r irr-plot, fig.cap = "Annualized IRR of the loans by risk category."}
percent <- function(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")
ggplot(subset(results, irr < 0.4),
       aes(x = irr,
           y = risk.cat)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "gray70",
               outlier.alpha = .5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0,
             colour = 2, linetype = 2, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(transform = "log1p",
                     labels = percent) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(y = "Risk Category", x = "IRR (annualized)")
```
